Given a doubly linked list where each node has two references (prev and next): one that points to a previous node and another that points to a next node. Assume the linked list below and provide the output for the following two lines.

The list is restored to its initial state before each line executes:

Line1: printf(“%d”, head->next->next->next->prev->prev->data);
Line2: printf(“%d”, tail->prev->prev->prev->prev->next->next->data);

Which of the options is correct.

options.text: Output of line $1$ is $7$ and Output of line $2$ is $9$
Output of line $1$ is $9$ and Output of line $2$ is $7$

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Answer: A

Line1: head->next->next->next->prev->prev->data;

head → next is a pointer to node containing the value 7.

Similarly head → next → next → next is pointer to node containing 5.

node(5) → prev → prev is pointer to node containing 7.

node(7) → data = 7

Line2: tail->prev->prev->prev->prev->next->next->data;

tail is the pointer to node containing 1.

node(1) → prev → prev → prev → prev is the pointer to node containing 3.

node(3) → next → next is the pointer to node containing 9.

node(9) → data = 9.

Consider a mutual pair of recursive functions g() and h().

int g(struct node *l) {
 if (l == NULL || l->next == NULL) return 1;

Consider the following function Merge() that takes the head of two linked lists.

struct node {
 int value;
 struct node *next;
};
typedef struct node Node;
Node * Merge(Node * head1, Node * head2) {
 if (head1 == NULL) return head2;
 if (head2 == NULL) return head1;
 Node * head = NULL;
 if (head1 -> value < head2 -> value) {
 head = head1;
 head -> next = Merge(head1 -> next, head2);
 }
 else if (head1 -> value > head2 -> value) {
 head = head2;
 head -> next = Merge(head1, head2 -> next);
 }
return head;
}

Assume that the input lists are correctly sorted. Which of the following are some of the possible behaviors when Merge() is executed with well-formed and valid inputs? Correctly merged linked list is merged sorted linked list.

options.text: The function will produce a correctly merged linked list.
The function may lead to a null pointer dereference.
The function may result in an incorrectly merged linked list.
Merge() will work on the following two lists. <ul> <li>$\text{List}1: 1 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 5\rightarrow 7\rightarrow \text{Null}$

questions.solution:
Answer: C, D

Source solution 1 (score: 77)

The input to merge() is two pointer of type node.

(For the sake of this discussion we’ll limit ourselves to only discuss the case where both pointers belong to different LL).

When both pointers are not NULL, the function creates a new pointer “head” which copies the address of one of the input pointer which points to some node that has strictly lesser value than that of the other and returns this “head” pointer.

This means the merge() will always returns the pointer to the node which has strictly lesser value out of the two node pointers that it received.

Then merge() calls itself with the pointer of next node of selected node and same pointer of other node and merge() will save whatever address of the next merge() call returns in current head->next.

This means the merge() will recursively keep rearranging the resultant LL such that the order is always strictly increasing.

(We’ll see why this strictly word comes in again and again later)

When one of the pointers is NULL, then merge() returns the other pointer.

This means there are no more elements in one of the LL so it simply returns the other LL node pointer. Since, both input LL are already sorted, there’s no need to check further. It directly appends the remaining nodes of non-empty LL into the resultant LL.

When both the pointers are NULL, then merge() returns NULL.

This means there are no more elements in both LL, so it returns NULL.

Both the above conditions are our base case conditions to end the recursion (in favorable conditions).

*** So far so good ***

Now, suppose both input pointers point to some node with have same value. Then both if and else if condition will fail. And we’ll directly return NULL (since no assignment happened to head).

This means if both LL has distinct values in their nodes then the merge() correctly merges both LL in sorted order.

But if both LL has at least one value common in their nodes. Then resultant LL will only contain nodes which are less than that common value.

For example –

List1 → 2 → 4 → 6 → 8 → 10 → 12 → NULL

List1 → 5 → 10 → 15 → 20 → 25 → NULL

List = merge(List1, List2)

Then List → 2 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 8 → NULL

Answer :- C, D.

This is a classic problem involving recursive linked list manipulation. To find the correct behavior, we need to trace the logic carefully, specifically looking for edge cases.

Logic Analysis

The function Merge() is designed to merge two sorted linked lists. However, there is a significant logical flaw in the conditional statements:

  1. Case 1: head1->value < head2->value — This is handled correctly.

  2. Case 2: head1->value > head2->value — This is handled correctly.

  3. Case 3: head1->value == head2->value — This is NOT handled.

If two nodes have the same value, the function skips both the if and else if blocks. Since head was initialized to NULL, the function simply returns NULL. This means that if the lists contain equal values, the merging process will terminate prematurely and return a truncated list.

Evaluation of OptionsA. The function will produce a correctly merged linked list.

Incorrect. While it might work for lists with strictly unique values, it fails to "correctly" merge in the general sense because it cannot handle lists with overlapping/equal values.

B. The function may lead to a null pointer dereference.

Incorrect. Let's look at the access points:

  • head1->value and head2->value: These are safe because the function returns early if head1 or head2 is NULL.

  • head->next = Merge(...): While Merge might return NULL (due to the equality bug), assigning NULL to a pointer is a perfectly valid operation. It does not dereference the null pointer; it simply ends the list there.

C. The function may result in an incorrectly merged linked list.

Correct. As identified, if any node in List1 has the same value as a node in List2 (or even within the same list if the logic were slightly different), the function returns NULL. The resulting list would be missing all subsequent nodes, making it "incorrectly merged."

D. Merge() will work on the following two lists.

  • List 1: $1 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow \text{Null}$

  • List 2: $2 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 12 \rightarrow \text{Null}$

Correct. In this specific case, all values in both lists are distinct. Because there are no instances where head1->value == head2->value, the code will always enter either the < or the > block. Consequently, the recursion will complete successfully, and the lists will be merged perfectly.

Summary

The correct options are C and D. The function works for unique-value inputs but fails logically for inputs containing duplicates.

To determine the final linked list returned by the function foo(), we need to trace the recursive calls and the "unwinding" process where the pointers are actually rearranged.

Function Logic Analysis

The function foo() performs a recursive weaving (interleaving) of two linked lists:

  • Base Cases: If either list is empty, it returns the other list.

  • Recursive Step: It calls itself with the next pointers of both current heads.

  • Rearrangement (Post-recursion): After the recursive call returns a pointer (temp), it sets head1->next to head2, and head2->next to temp. It then returns the original head1.

Execution Trace

Given:

  • List 1 ($L_1$): $1 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 9 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$

  • List 2 ($L_2$): $2 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$

1. Recursive Calls (Going Down)

  • Call 1: foo(1, 2) $\rightarrow$ calls foo(3, 4)

  • Call 2: foo(3, 4) $\rightarrow$ calls foo(5, 8)

  • Call 3: foo(5, 8) $\rightarrow$ calls foo(7, 10)

  • Call 4: foo(7, 10) $\rightarrow$ calls foo(9, NULL)

  • Call 5: foo(9, NULL) $\rightarrow$ Base Case Hit. head2 is NULL, so it returns head1 (the sublist $9 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$).

2. Pointer Rearrangement (Coming Up)

Now we "unwind" the recursion stack, applying the logic head1->next = head2 and head2->next = temp.

  • Return to Call 4 (head1=7, head2=10, temp=9):

    • 7->next = 10

    • 10->next = 9

    • Current sequence: $7 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 9 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$

  • Return to Call 3 (head1=5, head2=8, temp=7):

    • 5->next = 8

    • 8->next = 7

    • Current sequence: $5 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 9 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$

  • Return to Call 2 (head1=3, head2=4, temp=5):

    • 3->next = 4

    • 4->next = 5

    • Current sequence: $3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 9 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$

  • Return to Call 1 (head1=1, head2=2, temp=3):

    • 1->next = 2

    • 2->next = 3

    • Final sequence: $1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 8 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow 9 \rightarrow 10 \rightarrow \text{NULL}$

Conclusion

The final interleaved list is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 7, 10, 9, 10.

The correct option is C.
